Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A method is provided comprising the steps of exciting a vibration mode of a flow tube (130, 130′), wherein first and second drivers (180L, 180R) are amplitude modulated out of phase from each other, and wherein a drive command provided to the first and second drivers (180L, 180R) comprises a sum of N+1 independent signals. The first and second drivers (180L, 180R) are excited with a plurality of off-resonance frequencies and the effective phase between a modal response and the drivers (180L, 180R) at each of the off-resonance frequencies is inferred. A left eigenvector phase estimate is generated for each of the off-resonance frequencies. A phase of a left eigenvector at a resonant drive frequency is estimated based on off-resonance frequency phase estimates. The method also comprises measuring the phase between a first pickoff (170L) and a second pickoff (170R) and determining a phase of a right eigenvector for the flow tube (130, 130′).

outputs.L1: A method is provided comprising the steps of exciting a vibration mode of a flow tube (130, 130′), wherein first and second drivers (180L, 180R) are amplitude-modulated out of phase with each other, and a drive command supplied to the first and second drivers (180L, 180R) comprises a sum of N+1 independent signals. The first and second drivers (180L, 180R) are excited at a plurality of off-resonance frequencies, and the effective phase between a modal response and the drivers (180L, 180R) is inferred at each off-resonance frequency. A left-eigenvector phase estimate is generated for each off-resonance frequency, and the phase of a left eigenvector at a resonant drive frequency is estimated based on the off-resonance frequency phase estimates. outputs.L2: A method includes inducing a vibrational mode in a flow tube (130, 130′) by amplitude-modulating first and second drivers (180L, 180R) in opposite phases. The drive command supplied to the two drivers (180L, 180R) is formed from the sum of N+1 mutually independent signals. The drivers are actuated at multiple off-resonant frequencies, and, for each such frequency, the effective phase relationship between the drivers (180L, 180R) and the resulting modal response is derived. A left-eigenvector phase estimate is then produced for every off-resonant frequency. Using these off-resonance estimates, the phase of the left eigenvector at the resonant drive frequency is estimated. The method further includes measuring the phase difference between a first pickoff (170L) and a second pickoff (170R) and using that measurement to determine the phase of a right eigenvector associated with the flow tube (130, 130′).
outputs.L3:
A vibration mode of a flow tube is excited by first and second drivers. The drivers receive amplitude-modulated excitation signals that are out of phase with one another, thereby producing a controlled modal response in the flow tube. The drive command supplied to the two drivers is formed from a sum of \(N+1\) independent signals, allowing the tube to be excited simultaneously or sequentially at multiple frequencies.

At least some of these excitation frequencies are selected to be off resonance. The resulting modal responses are measured and used to infer the effective phase relationship between the flow-tube mode and the two drivers. In particular, estimates of the left eigenvector phase are obtained at the off-resonance frequencies. These phase estimates are then used, for example through fitting or interpolation, to estimate the left eigenvector phase at the resonant drive frequency.

The system also measures the phase difference between two pickoff signals associated with the vibrating flow tube. This measured pickoff-to-pickoff phase is used to determine the phase of a right eigenvector of the flow tube. Together, the estimated left eigenvector phase and the measured right eigenvector phase provide information characterizing the tube’s vibrational behavior at resonance.
outputs.L4:
A method is provided for analyzing a resonant mode of a flow tube using two independently controlled vibration drivers and at least two vibration pickoffs. The drivers apply amplitude-modulated excitation forces to the flow tube, with the modulation of one driver arranged out of phase with that of the other. A drive command containing \(N+1\) independent signals is used to excite and identify the relevant modal components of a system having \(N\) measured responses. By separating the responses associated with the independent command signals, the method distinguishes the contribution of each driver and obtains sufficient information to characterize the mode without relying solely on measurements taken exactly at resonance.

The flow tube is excited at multiple frequencies displaced from the resonant frequency. At each off-resonance excitation frequency, the amplitudes and phases of the resulting pickoff signals are measured relative to the applied drive signals. The measurements are combined with a dynamic model of the tube to infer the phases of the modal responses. Because the two drivers are amplitude modulated in opposite phase, their respective effects can be separated even when they act simultaneously. The collection of off-resonance measurements therefore provides estimates of the phase relationships associated with the mode’s left eigenvector, which describes how the applied forces couple into that mode.

The left-eigenvector phase estimates obtained at the different excitation frequencies are then processed, for example by interpolation, fitting, or model-based extrapolation, to determine the left-eigenvector phase at the resonant frequency. This approach avoids ambiguities and measurement difficulties that can occur when attempting to determine the drive-side modal phase directly at resonance.

The response-side modal behavior is determined from the relative phase of the signals produced by the two pickoffs. In particular, the phase difference between the pickoff responses at or near resonance establishes the phase relationship of the mode’s right eigenvector, which describes the vibration pattern of the flow tube. Combining the resonant left-eigenvector phase with the right-eigenvector information provides a comprehensive characterization of the resonant mode, including both the manner in which the drivers excite the mode and the manner in which the resulting motion appears at the pickoffs. This characterization may be used to improve modal identification, drive control, calibration, diagnostic monitoring, and measurement accuracy in a vibrating flow-tube instrument.

### The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the most common words in the English language. Although it consists of only three letters, it plays an essential role in communication. As the definite article, “the” identifies a specific person, place, object, or idea. For example, “a book” may refer to any book, while “the book” points to a particular one.

This small word helps make language precise and understandable. It allows speakers and writers to distinguish the known from the unknown and the general from the specific. We use it in everyday expressions such as “the sun,” “the world,” and “the future.”

Because it appears so frequently, “the” often goes unnoticed. Yet without it, many English sentences would sound incomplete or unclear. Its simplicity shows that even the smallest words can have great importance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style method claim for determining left and right eigenvector phases in a vibrating flow tube using out-of-phase amplitude-modulated drivers, off-resonance excitation frequencies, and two pickoffs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a method for modal phase estimation in a Coriolis flowmeter, preserving component reference numerals such as flow tube (130, 130′), drivers (180L, 180R), and pickoffs (170L, 170R).
counterfactuals.output:
A method for modal phase estimation in a Coriolis flowmeter includes:

1. Vibrating the flow tube (130, 130′) using one or both drivers (180L, 180R), typically near a selected resonant mode.
2. Receiving motion signals from the left and right pickoffs (170L, 170R), which represent the vibration response of the flow tube (130, 130′).
3. Decomposing or combining the pickoff signals according to the expected mode shape to isolate a modal response and suppress contributions from other modes, asymmetry, and noise.
4. Determining the phase of the isolated modal response relative to the excitation applied through the drivers (180L, 180R), for example by synchronous detection or complex frequency-domain estimation.
5. Calculating a modal phase difference from the phases associated with the pickoffs (170L, 170R) and/or drivers (180L, 180R).
6. Using the estimated modal phase difference to determine a flow-related quantity, such as mass flow rate, while optionally compensating for tube imbalance, coupling between modes, damping, or changing operating conditions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single technical paragraph describing how to estimate the phase of a left eigenvector at resonance from multiple off-resonance phase measurements and determine the right eigenvector phase from two pickoff signals.
counterfactuals.output: To estimate the phase of a left eigenvector at a resonance frequency \(\omega_r\), unwrap the phases measured at several frequencies on both sides of resonance, correct them for known channel delays and transfer-function phases, fit the resulting off-resonance phase data with a smooth local model (typically a weighted linear or low-order polynomial fit versus frequency), and evaluate the fit at \(\omega_r\); the fit uncertainty provides the phase-estimation error, while a fixed normalization or reference channel removes the otherwise arbitrary global eigenvector phase. The right eigenvector phase can then be obtained from two coherent pickoff signals \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) by forming their calibrated complex ratio, so that \(\Delta\phi_R=\arg[(p_2/H_2)/(p_1/H_1)]\), where \(H_1\) and \(H_2\) are the respective pickoff transfer functions; assigning one right-eigenvector component zero phase fixes the convention, and the other component has phase \(\Delta\phi_R\), modulo \(2\pi\).
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide an abstract-like description of a flow-tube modal analysis method that uses first and second drivers, multifrequency off-resonance excitation, left eigenvector phase estimates, and a measured phase difference between first and second pickoffs.
counterfactuals.output: A flow-tube modal analysis method employs first and second drivers to apply multifrequency, off-resonance excitation to a vibrating flow tube. Responses are acquired at first and second pickoffs and represented in a frequency-domain dynamic model. Left eigenvectors of the identified system are used to estimate the modal response phase at each pickoff while reducing sensitivity to drive amplitude, actuator dynamics, and modal overlap. For each excitation frequency, a measured phase difference between the first and second pickoff signals is compared with, or combined with, the corresponding left-eigenvector phase estimates. Data from multiple off-resonance frequencies and both drivers are jointly processed to determine modal parameters, including mode shape, natural frequency, damping, and phase relationships. The resulting analysis supports robust characterization of flow-tube dynamics without requiring excitation directly at resonance.
